description_full: Graham Corporation designs and manufactures fluid, power, heat transfer, and vacuum technologies for chemical and petrochemical processing, defense, space, petroleum refining, cryogenic, and energy industries. The company offers power plant systems, including ejectors and surface condensers, as well as torpedo ejection, propulsion, and power systems comprising turbines, alternators, regulators, pumps, and blowers for the defense industry. It also provides heat transfer and vacuum systems that include ejectors, process and surface condensers, liquid ring pumps, and heat exchangers, as well as nozzles and power generation systems, such as turbines, generators, compressors, and pumps for the energy and process industry. In addition, the company offers rocket propulsion systems, including turbopumps, fuel, cryogenic, and nuclear propellant pumps; cooling systems comprising pumps, compressors, fans, and blowers; and life support systems that consist of fans, pumps, and blowers for the space industry. Further, it provides thermal management systems, such as pumps, blowers, and electronics for the defense and energy sector; advanced mixing systems, including bladeless centrifugal mixers, accessories, services, and consumables; and spare parts for its equipment. It serves customers in the United States, Asia, Canada, the Middle East, South America, and internationally. Graham Corporation was founded in 1936 and is headquartered in Batavia, New York.

financial_summary: Graham Corporation is a small-cap industrials business with a $979M market cap on $245M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 6% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.
The company is burning through $121,000 of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.3× net debt/EBITDA.
Net dilution runs at 0.1% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 5.1% of the shares.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.55x).
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+25.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 33% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 23% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 57% and a beta of 1.05, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.11 vs 5y 1.10), so read it loosely.
About $14.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 50% in the 2020 crash, 52% in the 2022 bear market and 86% in 2008.
val: The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 95%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 72.5 vs 24.1 and EV/EBITDA 34.1 vs 13.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 35% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -0.0% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $122 on average, 47% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.64).
It runs a 24% gross margin and burns cash (FCF margin -0%).
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.27x, but a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
ROE of 9% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 6pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 2.6% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.3x net debt to EBITDA ($6.6M of cash against $13.0M of debt).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.0% over 3 years, 20.3% over 5 years and 10.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 1.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.49 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 2.2x annual revenue and deferred revenue up 22%.
Capex runs 2.0x depreciation (6.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 5.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 93%.
The share count has grown 2.0% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 732 employees, each generates about $335K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 5.9% a year across its filed history.
CEO pay is $1.2M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
